source_sentences: The Regulations create six national licenses of 20 MHz in the 2.9 GHz band, sold to bidders who qualify by deposit.
It is an ascending clock auction with a reserve of M40 million a block.
The term is 15 years, with no right of renewal ("the Authority may re-auction or renew at market value").

The Regulations were announced and made on 1 March 2027, the auction ran in September and October 2027, licenses take effect on 1 January 2028, the coverage deadline is 31 December 2032 and licenses expire on 31 December 2042.
"Payments under these Regulations shall be paid into the Consolidated Fund." The Treasury receives the auction payments.
Each licensee must provide service in the band to areas containing 90% of the population by 31 December 2032, or the license is revoked without refund.
The TCA enforces: coverage is verified by drive tests and operators' coverage maps; a licensee that has not met the coverage obligation by the deadline has its license revoked, without refund.

Covering 90% of the population with this band takes about 6,500 sites per network; covering the cities and large towns (about 65% of the population), which operators said in consultation they would cover commercially within five years, takes about 3,000.
No more than two blocks may be awarded to, or held by, one person and its affiliates.
Affiliates are those where one controls more than 50%, or has the right to appoint a majority of the board.
The cap binds each bidder and later holder.

The TCA runs the auction and monitors coverage; its added costs are M9 million for the auction and M2 million a year for monitoring, funded by an increase in its annual appropriation from the general budget.

context: Tarnesse is a country of about 12 million people with its own currency, the mark (M).
Three mobile network operators serve it: Ardel Mobile (about 42% of subscriptions), Nevra Telecom (36%) and Kostel (22%).
Mobile data traffic grows about 30% a year, and busy-hour capacity in the cities is tight; without new spectrum, operators add capacity by adding cell sites in their existing bands ("densification").
Fixed broadband: Linmark Fibre passes about 25% of homes with fibre; Pellow Networks' copper (DSL) lines serve about 1.6 million households, including about 700,000 outside fibre and cable areas.
There are about 11,000 tower and rooftop sites, most owned by two tower companies (Selwyn Towers and Haldmoor Sites); new towers need municipal permits that take 4 to 9 months.
About 1,400 certified tower riggers do about 3,000 site installations a year.
All radio equipment is imported; Tarnesse buys about 0.4% of the world's mobile radio equipment.
Under the Radio Act, no one may transmit on spectrum without a license.
Five bidders qualified: the three operators, Linmark Fibre (which plans fixed wireless access outside its fibre footprint) and Ombra Group (a foreign operator seeking entry).
